items.question: What is Memory Chess?
items.answer: Memory Chess is a free board-memory game. You study a chess position for a short time, rebuild it from memory, and get a score based on how many pieces you placed correctly.

items.question: How do I play?
items.answer: Choose how many pieces you want and how long you want to study the board. When the position disappears, place the pieces back on the squares you remember. Submit your answer to see your accuracy and time.

items.question: Can beginners play Memory Chess?
items.answer: Yes. You do not need to know chess openings or calculate moves. Start with fewer pieces and more study time, then make the game harder when you feel ready.

items.question: How does it train chess visualization?
items.answer: Each round gives you focused practice holding a chess position in your mind and recalling where the pieces belong. Your score shows which positions feel easy and where you need more practice.

items.question: What should I look for when memorizing the board?
items.answer: Start with easy anchors such as kings, queens, corners, and edge squares. Then look for groups, lines, diagonals, and empty spaces instead of trying to remember every piece on its own.

items.question: How can I make the game harder?
items.answer: Add more pieces, shorten the study time, or hide the board coordinates. Change one setting at a time so you can see what makes the biggest difference.

items.question: Is Memory Chess free?
items.answer: Yes. You can play for free without creating an account. Adding a name to the leaderboard is optional.

items.question: How often should I practice?
items.answer: A few focused rounds on a regular schedule is a good place to start. Keep sessions short enough that you can still study each position carefully.

notebook.title: You can't improve what you never measure.
notebook.lede: Most chess practice trains decisions. Very little of it checks whether you can actually hold the board in your head. That skill sits under calculation, blindfold play and spotting tactics, and it is usually left to chance.

observation.title: Players lose track of pieces mid-calculation.
observation.body: Three moves deep, a bishop on the long diagonal quietly disappears from the picture in your head. The board in front of you was right. The one in your mind was not.

hypothesis.title: Board recall is a trainable, testable skill.
hypothesis.body: Hold a position briefly, rebuild it, check the result. Repeat with more pieces and less time. <hl>We make no claims about your brain.</hl> We give you a reading you can track.

method.title: One round, one clean number.
method.body: Study, blank board, rebuild, score. Right squares are marked, wrong squares are marked, nothing is hidden. Rounds take under a minute, so you can run many.

method.title: A round, under the microscope.
method.lede: Scroll through one round on a real position: the end of Kasparov's Immortal, Kasparov against Topalov at Wijk aan Zee in 1999. The overlays show one way to memorise it, not a recording of anyone's attention.

standoff.name: Stand-off
standoff.sentence: White's king hits d2. Black's king and c3 guard it.

mirror.name: Stairs
mirror.sentence: Mirror stairs, h2 up to f4, h7 down to f5.

longShots.name: Long shots
longShots.sentence: Queen a7 eyes h7. Rook d2 eyes h2.

study.name: Study
study.title: Eleven pieces, ten seconds.
study.body: The final position of Kasparov's Immortal, after 44.Qa7. Topalov resigned here. Take in the whole board, not square by square. In de Groot's experiments, masters reproduced a briefly shown game position far better than weaker players.
study.note: Fig. White: king c1, queen a7, pawns f4, g3, h2. Black: king e1, rook d2, pawns c3, f5, g6, h7.

anchors.name: Anchors
anchors.title: Start with the kings.
anchors.body: Fix two points first. Both kings sit on the first rank, two files apart, and Black's king has run all the way to e1. Place everything else relative to them.
anchors.note: Fig. the two kings ringed. Everything else waits.

chunk.name: Chunk
chunk.title: Eleven pieces become three ideas.
chunk.body: Group pieces by what they do to each other. The kings fight over d2. Two pawn staircases meet. The queen and rook each aim at an unguarded h-pawn. Chase and Simon (1973) found that strong players recall positions in chunks of related pieces.
chunk.note: Fig. orange attacks, blue defends, grey joins a pawn chain, the bar marks a blocked pair. The rook on d2 sits in two groups.

encode.name: Encode
encode.title: Turn each group into a sentence.
encode.body: Name each group by its job. Gobet and Simon (1996) describe strong players holding larger, schema-like structures. The sentences themselves are a technique, not a research finding.
encode.note: Fig. the three groups, named. Their sentences:

blank.name: Blank
blank.title: The board clears.
blank.body: No pieces, no hints. Rebuild from the sentences, not from a picture. Say them in order: the kings first, then each group.
blank.note: Nothing to do here but hold three sentences.

rebuild.name: Rebuild
rebuild.title: Rebuild group by group.
rebuild.body: Kings. The stand-off. The stairs. The long shots. Place each group with its sentence before you start the next.
rebuild.note: Fig. the rebuild before it is checked. One pawn is on the wrong square. Can you see which?

score.name: Score
score.title: Check it against your sentences, then score.
score.body: Re-check each relation on the rebuilt board. Is the rook still held twice? From c2 the pawn guards d1, not d2. The count, five and six, still matches, so only the relation check catches the slip.
score.note: Fig. ticks still hold, the red cross broke. Orange fill is the wrong square (c2), the ring is where it belonged (c3). {correct} of {total} squares is {accuracy}%.

meta.description: Profiles of chess players and memory researchers. Each one gives the documented feat, the research that explains it, and a drill to try.

list.heading: Articles
list.sub: Chess players and memory researchers, one profile at a time.
list.about1: Each article follows one chess player or researcher and one question about their memory. The subject may be a player known for a feat of recall, or a researcher who measured what players remember after a few seconds.
list.about2: Every article has the same parts. A portrait comes with its photographer and licence. A fact file gives the dates, the titles and the memory feat the person is known for. The story sets that feat beside the research that explains it. A source list shows where each claim comes from. A drill at the end opens a round of Memory Chess with the piece count and viewing time the story suggests.
list.about3: The articles are researched and drafted with AI assistance from published sources such as interviews, tournament reports, books and research papers. A separate check then compares every date, number and quotation with those sources before anything is published. Where sources disagree, the article says who reported what. An anecdote that sources report only as a story is told as a story. Articles in other languages are translated from the English text with AI assistance, and each translation is checked before it goes up.

reference.title: How the daily board works
reference.shared: Every day at midnight UTC a new position is drawn, and every player in the world gets the same one. The position comes from a seed made from the date, so nobody can see it early and nobody gets an easier copy. Because the board is shared, a score on it means the same thing for everyone who played it that day.
reference.oneTry: You get one try. Opening the board counts as the try, so leaving during the study phase and coming back does not show it to you twice. Your device remembers the try until the next board opens.
reference.grid: After you rebuild the position you see which squares you got right, which held the wrong piece, which you missed and where you placed an extra piece. The share row lists one square per piece, sorted by outcome, with nothing about where it stood, so posting it does not give the board away to someone who has not played yet.
reference.join: To join the board, pick a name of 4 to 16 characters and the country you play for. The country starts from the one you picked before, then from your connection, then from your browser's language, and you can always change it. Your rating at the moment you join is shown beside your name.
reference.ranking: Rows are ranked by the number of pieces placed correctly, then by the fewest wrong pieces, then by the fastest rebuild. Everyone studies for the same number of seconds, so study time never separates two players on the daily board.
reference.arcTitle: Pieces and study time through the week
reference.arcIntro: The setting follows a weekly arc. Monday starts gently so a weekend break does not end a streak, the load builds through the week, Saturday is a flash board you see for only a few seconds, and Sunday is the hardest board of all. Within each day's range the date picks one setting, the same for every player.
